opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
For quite a while, I haven't written any reflections for Hope and Prayer. Life has been full. The pool service business has kept me busy, occupied, and distracted. I tell myself I have my priorities straight... but do I?

How easy it is to allow life to get in the way of what matters most.
Yet as I sit down and read today's readings, my mind begins to quiet, and my heart takes over.
Yes, I have been busy, but that doesn't mean I love Jesus any less.

In the Book of Zechariah 9:9–10, we hear the prophecy that the King is coming. In Psalm 145 we proclaim, "I will praise your name forever, my King and my God." Then comes the invitation: "Let all your works give you thanks, O Lord, and let your faithful ones bless you."

As I read those words, I immediately think of my husband. Lately, we've been working side by side on a particularly difficult pool project. Under pressure, when things are going wrong, I hear him quietly tell God that he loves Him and thanks Him—in every circumstance.

It reminds me that our works can give thanks to God and that our lives can bless Him.
How can we bless God?

He is all-powerful. He lacks nothing. Yet somehow He delights in the love, trust, gratitude, and obedience of His children. We bless Him when our hearts turn toward Him. We bless Him when we thank Him instead of complaining, when we trust Him instead of ourselves, and when we love Him in both peaceful moments and difficult ones.

Then the second reading, Epistle to the Romans 8:9, 11–13, reminds us that we are not living according to the flesh but according to the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells within us. We are no longer debtors to the flesh.

What a freeing thought.
When I say those words out loud, it's as though a blanket of relief wraps around me. I can breathe again.

Then comes the Gospel from Gospel of Matthew 11:25–30:

"Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for yourselves. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."

Before reading these passages, I had been quietly criticizing myself for not writing these reflections more consistently. I was measuring myself by what I hadn't done instead of receiving what Christ was offering.

Should I write more often?

Of course.

But should I carry guilt because I haven't?

No.

When I write, it isn't out of obligation. It comes from the heart. My mind certainly searches for the right words, but my heart is the one speaking.

And when the words come from Him, the burden is light.

It is only when I think according to the flesh—with its endless commitments, expectations, deadlines, and self-imposed pressures—that everything begins to feel heavy. I become disappointed in myself for what I didn't accomplish instead of grateful for what God is doing within me.

Jesus reminds me that His way is different.

I don't have to earn His love through productivity. I don't have to prove my devotion by checking another task off my list.

Our God is omnipotent. I come before Him humbly, not as someone wise or learned, but simply as His daughter. And He has not hidden Himself from me.

So today I choose not to dwell on what I have failed to do or what I think I should have done.

Instead, I will praise Him.

I will bless Him.

I will thank Him in every circumstance.

And I will seek my rest in Jesus, because it is there—and only there—that I feel most at peace.

His burden is light.

It is my flesh, and the thoughts that come from it, that are heavy.
